svg.title: Stall speed rises with load factor
svg.desc: Bars for an aircraft with a normal unaccelerated stalling speed of 50 knots: it stalls at 50 knots at 1 G, 100 knots at a load factor of 4 Gs, and would stall at 150 knots at 9 Gs. Cards give the bank angles from the text: significant beyond about 45 degrees, stalling speed up by about one half at about 63 degrees, load factor 3 above 72 degrees so a 45 knot aircraft must stay above 75 knots. High speed stalls: 1.7 times stalling speed gives 3 Gs and 112 knots gives 4 Gs with a 60 knot stalling speed.
svg.text: Stall speed rises with load factor
An aircraft's stalling speed increases in proportion to the square root of the load factor, so a
banked turn or abrupt pull up can stall it at a seemingly safe speed.
An aircraft that stalls at 50 knots in unaccelerated flight
1 G
stalls at 50 knots
4 Gs
stalls at 100 knots
9 Gs
stalls at 150 knots
(only if it could withstand a load factor of nine)
Bar lengths are drawn to the knots shown.
Banked turns
Load factor becomes significant to performance and
wing structure beyond approximately 45° of bank
At approximately 63° of bank, stalling speed is
increased by approximately one-half
Banking more than 72° in a steep turn gives a load
factor of 3: with a normal stalling speed of 45
knots, keep the airspeed above 75 knots
High speed stalls
The only way to stall above normal stalling speed
is to add load factor, such as a severe pull on the
elevator
At 1.7 times stalling speed (about 102 knots when
the stalling speed is 60 knots) the load factor is
3 Gs
At 112 knots in the same aircraft it is 4 Gs
Why it matters
Danger of inadvertently stalling by raising the
load factor, as in a steep turn or spiral
A quick pull up or any maneuver above 1 G has the
same effect
Structure
Because the load factor is squared as the stalling
speed doubles, tremendous loads can be imposed by
stalling at high airspeeds
Older light airplanes: design maneuvering speed is
approximately 1.7 times normal stalling speed; 60
knots x 1.7 = 102 knots, 2.89 Gs
Abrupt back elevator near the ground, particularly in a steep turn, has caused many accidents. Check your
own airplane's numbers in the AFM/POH.
